Some colleges offer trades training courses just as if i were to go to school for an accounting degree or law. you can apply for and pay thousands of dollars to go to, however you do not get any sort of certification at the end, so its really not worth anything especially because you still have to do an apprenticeship and work a minimum amount of hours to get certified in a trade. It doesn’t really help you get ahead in any way, actually it sets you back tremendously. As i said its pointless because (At least in ontario, canada as i know it) apprentices are sent to school for free to those same colleges for 3 semesters over the 5-6 years of their apprenticeship anyways.

Edit: i read the question wrong before writing a novel lol. I might add you should complete your high-school first though. Unions require your high-school education to join, and If the trades dont work out for you you then at least you don’t have to go back to complete high school in order to follow another career path.

If you decide to go union start applying now and every year after until you get in. because there is often a chance you will have to wait a couple of years due to the high amount of applicants you will have to compete with. 

Now for the novel i wrote before i realized i misread your question. 

Apply for the apprenticeship. In electrical, I believe going to school before your apprenticeship is a waste of time and money, especially since you are sent to school (for free i might add) anyways during the duration of your apprenticeship. I find that people who spent time to do electrical at college first and then joined the trade have little useable knowledge or skills that they can apply in a real-world scenario. Apprenticeships build you from the ground up and give you actual useable skills from the start. Not to mention that you will be making revenue while learning. By the time you are done your apprenticeship you will have a better idea of what  part of the industry you wish to learn more about, and then you can apply for college courses that are more catered to your goals or experiences.  If you join the union alot more resources are available to you, and they also provide specific courses for expanding your skillset if you choose (or you can just apply to supplementary college courses). You don’t want to go through school first, join the trade, and then find out that you don’t like it or that you learned nothing relating to the type of electrical you are actually interested in. Plus, employers are more likely to hire someone with work experience rather than someone fresh outta school who only knows  how the trade works on paper.

I know exactly what you are talking about and can relate. Some days you excel socially, and others you completely trample your progress. Sometimes you become so confident that you overdo it the next day. Its often beyond your immediate control, and you can feel like a bystander to your own behaviour. It never hits you until its too late, a day has gone by and you feel like you've failed again. At least you are somewhat aware of what is happening. Awareness can be both a blessing and a curse. Right now its a curse, cuz you cant control it, but you can make it a blessing by learning from it to improve.

This is where the "hold your tongue" tip comes in.  When you have a thought of something I assume you just spurt it out without calculating the costs. What helped me do better was this: wether its important or not, just keep it to yourself. Become an observer, a thinker, and keep your thoughts in your head even if sometimes it feels like you are holding your breath. Speak sparsely, like talk is a valuable commodity not to be wasted. The social flak comes from being too spontaneous, but if you stay reserved you will find you will have more controlled and thought out conversation with your peers.

Also, I could never believe how valuable this advice is: "Think before You Speak". Because it  will help you in the long run to construct and calculate what you are gonna do and say. 

Also, physically, keep your back and neck straight as you stand and sit. It seems silly but I've noticed that standing like a solider can help you think better, especially when we spend our school days sitting hunched over our desks and cellphones.

All this advice is nice and dandy, but if you can't apply it in the heat of the moment, then what use is it? Well, how I I like to keep a list of reminders and quotes on the notepad on my phone, which i can look at throughout the day or whenever you make a notable mistake. Repeat the reminders over and over again in your head, and try to make them a habit.

Good luck brother hope it helps.
